summary: The first proposal for a file transfer protocol on the ARPANET, written at MIT Project MAC. It argues for indirect use of remote computers, where you move files between systems without logging in to each one and learning its quirks. It was a draft for discussion, later revised in RFC 172.

plainLanguage.summary: Instead of logging into each remote computer and learning its rules, RFC 114 proposed having a helper program move files between systems in a standard way.

subtitle: An early proposal for transferring files between ARPANET hosts without logging into each one.

tldr.problem: Using a remote computer directly meant logging in and learning its conventions, but users wanted to move files between different systems without doing so.
tldr.mechanism: The proposal describes cooperating processes that exchange 72-bit descriptor transactions (request, response, transfer, terminate) over a single full-duplex NCP connection. It defines operations such as retrieve, store, append, delete, rename, lookup, open, close and execute.
tldr.outcome: RFC 114 was a first-cut draft for discussion; it was updated by RFC 133, 141, 171 and 172 as FTP evolved. Its status is Unknown.

facts.label: Connection
facts.value: Single full-duplex NCP connection for data and control

sections.title: Direct and Indirect Use
sections.content: RFC 114 distinguishes direct use (logging into a remote host and using it like a local user, so you must know its conventions) from indirect use (an intermediate process hides differences so you only need standard file transfer commands). The protocol was developed for implementation on the GE645/Multics and PDP-10/DM/CG-ITS, and was intended to let users at any cooperating host use other hosts' file systems. It also covers running programs on remote hosts.
sections.plainLanguage: You could either travel to another computer and learn its rules, or ask a helper that knows the rules to fetch and send files for you.

sections.title: Transactions and Their Types
sections.content:
The protocol is built from transactions. Each transaction has a 72-bit descriptor (containing a 24-bit code, 8-bit filler count, NUL, 24-bit data count, NUL), followed by data and filler. The first byte of the code is the transaction type; the second is the data type. The four basic transaction types are request, response, transfer and terminate.

Request types include Identify, Retrieve, Store, Append, Delete, Rename, addname/deletename, Lookup, Open, Close and Execute. A host may implement only a subset and refuse others with an unsuccessful terminate. Error codes (such as Access denied or File search failed) are carried in unsuccessful terminates. Data types describe how to interpret data (for example network ASCII, EBCDIC, binary and various number formats).
sections.plainLanguage: Every message is labeled to say what it does and how much data it carries. The protocol defines basic operations like asking for a file, sending a file, or stopping.

sections.title: Transaction Sequences and Connections
sections.content:
A transaction sequence begins with a request and ends with a terminate. For Retrieve, the server sends rs (ready-to-send), then transfers the file, then sends a successful terminate. For Store, the server sends rr (ready-to-receive), the user sends the file, then the server terminates. Either host may abort at any time with an unsuccessful terminate; a more drastic abort uses CLS (close connection) in the middle of a transfer.

Cooperating processes listen on a prearranged NCP socket. A single full-duplex connection carries both data and control, established using the connection method of RFC 66 as modified by RFC 80. The first transaction from user to server is Identify, which identifies the user.
sections.plainLanguage: A file transfer follows a simple exchange: ask, get ready, move the file, say done. Both ends share one connection for control and data.

sections.title: Extensions and Notes
sections.content:
RFC 114 notes several possible extensions: access control (such as passwords), uniform file headings/attributes, broader use of the Execute command (including program mediation), and transaction sequence identification numbers to handle multiple requests simultaneously. It also observes that implementations may choose subsets, and recommends accepting network ASCII and binary data types at minimum.

Filler bits allow for systems where NCP only exchanges bytes rather than arbitrary bits. The 72-bit descriptor is chosen to align conveniently across common byte sizes on ARPANET hosts.
sections.plainLanguage: The design leaves room to add things like passwords, better descriptions of files, and more flexible ways to run remote programs.
